The question of whether subliminal advertising is real is genuinely contested across expert sources. [d1] takes a nuanced position, concluding "yes and no": while popular beliefs contain myths, subliminal advertising can influence consumers under certain conditions, particularly through stimuli presented below the threshold of conscious awareness. [d3] similarly cites psychologist Art Markman, who states subliminal advertising "can have some influence on a consumer, but it can't turn that person into a robot," and Philip Merikle, who points to studies showing "considerable information capable of informing decisions and guiding actions is perceived even when observers do not experience any awareness of perceiving."

However, other credible sources are far more skeptical. [d7] (Merriam-Webster) states plainly that "no such advertising has ever been shown to work," and [d9] (Vox) cites an expert who says "I don't think there's any evidence to suggest that it's more effective than just a traditional ad that we're very aware of," concluding it is probably not worth the investment for advertisers. [d6] (Forbes) describes the results of early subliminal advertising experiments as "scientifically disputed," noting there is evidence the messages worked "but not all the time." [d5] (Project MUSE) adds that there is "no real evidence that advertising agencies actually used subliminal techniques as a major means of communicating with consumers," suggesting the phenomenon was more myth than widespread practice. In sum, while subliminal perception as a psychological phenomenon has some research support [d1][d3], the effectiveness of subliminal advertising as a practical tool for changing consumer behavior remains scientifically disputed and unproven [d6][d7][d9].
